title: Unit 11: Electric Circuits

topics.name: Steady-state DC circuits
covers: Steady-state direct-current circuits with batteries and resistors only

guide.title: Electric circuits: review guide
guide.intro: This unit connects the microscopic picture of moving charge to resistance and power, then uses Kirchhoff's rules to analyze steady direct-current circuits.
guide.equationNote: e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Batteries are ideal unless an internal resistance is given.

sections.title: Current, drift, and current density
body: Current is the rate at which charge passes a point, I = dQ/dt. In a wire, I = nqAv_d, where n is the number of charge carriers per volume and v_d is their drift speed, typically far below a millimeter per second.
Conventional current points the way positive charge would flow, opposite to the electrons' drift. Current density J = I/A is related to the field in the material by J = E/ρ.
points: The electrical signal travels almost at light speed even though the electrons drift slowly.
Current is the same at every point in a single loop.
Current density points along the field in the conductor.

sections.title: Resistance and power
body: Resistance is R = ΔV/I. For a uniform wire, R = ρL/A. When the cross-section varies along the wire, add up thin slices: R = ∫ρ dx/A(x).
The power delivered to a resistor is P = IΔV = I²R = (ΔV)²/R, and for a steady current the energy over a time t is Pt.
points: Doubling the voltage across the same resistor quadruples its power.
Metals' resistivity usually rises with temperature.
Ohmic materials have a constant R; many devices don't.

sections.title: Steady-state DC circuits
body: Junction rule: the currents into a junction add up to the currents out. Loop rule: the potential changes around any closed loop add to zero. Together they solve any network of batteries and resistors.
A real battery has an internal resistance r, so its terminal voltage is ΔV = ε − Ir, which drops as it delivers more current.
points: In parallel, the smaller resistor carries more current and uses more power.
With several batteries in different branches, write junction and loop (or node) equations instead of combining resistors.
equations: terminal voltage of a real battery

example.prompt: A 9.0 V battery with internal resistance 0.50 Ω drives a 5.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 2.0 Ω resistors. Find the current and the battery's terminal voltage.
example.solution: The pair is equivalent to 1.0 Ω, so the total resistance is 0.50 + 5.0 + 1.0 = 6.5 Ω and I = 9.0/6.5 ≈ 1.38 A. Terminal voltage = 9.0 − (1.38)(0.50) ≈ 8.3 V.

misconceptions: “Electrons race through the wire at nearly light speed.”
Their drift speed is tiny; it is the field that sets up quickly.
Charge is conserved, so the current is the same all around a single loop.
A real battery's terminal voltage falls as it delivers more current.
“The largest resistor always uses the most power.”
In series it does (P = I²R); in parallel the smallest one does (P = (ΔV)²/R).

questions.prompt: A copper wire is 10 m long with a cross-sectional area of 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m². Copper's resistivity is 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m. What is the wire's resistance?
choiceExplanations: 5.9 is 1/R, the result inverted.
0.017 Ω uses a length of 1.0 m instead of 10 m.
1.7 × 10⁻¹³ multiplies by the area instead of dividing.

questions.prompt: A copper wire with cross-sectional area 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m² carries 2.0 A. Copper has 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per cubic meter. What is the electrons' drift speed? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.explanation: v_d = I/(nqA) = 2.0/((8.5 × 10²⁸)(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(1.0 × 10⁻⁶)) ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ m/s, a fraction of a millimeter per second.
choiceExplanations: 6.8 × 10³ is the reciprocal of the drift speed.
1.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ leaves out the cross-sectional area.
3.0 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light; the signal travels fast, but the electrons themselves drift slowly.

questions.prompt: A resistor uses 40 W when 20 V is across it. How much power does it use when 10 V is across it? (Its resistance doesn't change.)
questions.explanation: P = (ΔV)²/R. Halving the voltage divides the power by 2² = 4: 40 W ÷ 4 = 10 W. (R = 20²/40 = 10 Ω, and 10²/10 = 10 W.)
choiceExplanations: 20 W assumes power is proportional to voltage; it goes as voltage squared.
Lowering the voltage lowers the power.
The power changes when the voltage changes.

questions.prompt: A 12 V battery drives a 4.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω resistors. What current does the battery supply?
questions.explanation: The parallel pair is (6.0 × 3.0)/(6.0 + 3.0) = 2.0 Ω, so the total is 6.0 Ω and I = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A.
choiceExplanations: 3.0 A uses only the 4.0 Ω resistor.
6.0 A uses only the parallel pair, ignoring the 4.0 Ω resistor.
0.92 A treats all three resistors as being in series (13 Ω).

questions.prompt: A battery with emf 12 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω is connected to a 5.5 Ω resistor. What is the battery's terminal voltage?
choiceExplanations: 1.0 V is the drop across the internal resistance, not the terminal voltage.
12 V is the emf; part of it is lost across the internal resistance while current flows.
11.5 V subtracts the internal resistance itself (0.50) instead of the voltage across it (Ir = 1.0 V).

questions.prompt: Three branches connect points A and B. Branch 1 is a 10 V battery (positive terminal toward A) in series with 2.0 Ω. Branch 2 is a 4.0 V battery (positive terminal toward A) in series with 2.0 Ω. Branch 3 is a 4.0 Ω resistor. The batteries are ideal. What current flows through the 4.0 Ω resistor?
questions.explanation: Let V be the potential of A relative to B. Junction rule at A: (10 − V)/2.0 + (4.0 − V)/2.0 = V/4.0. Multiply by 4: 28 − 4V = V, so V = 5.6 V and the current in the 4.0 Ω resistor is 5.6/4.0 = 1.4 A.
choiceExplanations: 1.5 A puts the difference of the emfs, 6.0 V, across the 4.0 Ω resistor.
3.5 A adds the two emfs across the 4.0 Ω resistor alone, ignoring the branch resistors.
0.75 A treats the circuit as one loop with the emfs opposing; the 4.0 Ω resistor is a separate branch.

questions.prompt: A 6.0 Ω resistor and a 3.0 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. Which uses more power?
choices: The 3.0 Ω resistor: 48 W, versus 24 W for the 6.0 Ω resistor
They use the same power, 36 W each
Neither: in parallel, power doesn't depend on resistance
The 6.0 Ω resistor: 48 W, versus 24 W for the 3.0 Ω resistor
questions.explanation: Both have 12 V across them, so P = (ΔV)²/R: 144/3.0 = 48 W and 144/6.0 = 24 W. The smaller resistor carries more current and uses more power.
choiceExplanations: Same voltage across different resistances gives different powers.
With equal voltage, P = (ΔV)²/R depends directly on R.
P = I²R suggests the larger resistor wins only when the currents are equal, as in series; here the voltages are equal.

questions.prompt: A wire of length L and resistivity ρ has a cross-sectional area that grows steadily along its length: A(x) = A₀(1 + x/L), from A₀ at one end to 2A₀ at the other. What is its resistance?
questions.explanation: Add thin slices in series: R = ∫₀ᴸ ρ dx/(A₀(1 + x/L)) = (ρL/A₀) ln(1 + x/L) from 0 to L = (ρL/A₀) ln 2 ≈ 0.69ρL/A₀.
choiceExplanations: 2ρL/(3A₀) uses the average area, 1.5A₀; resistance adds up 1/A along the wire, which isn't the same.
ρL/(2A₀) uses the largest area for the whole wire.
ρL/A₀ uses the smallest area for the whole wire.

questions.prompt: In a wire, the free electrons drift toward the left. Which way does the conventional current point?
choices: There is no current, because electrons cancel the protons
It depends on the wire's resistance
questions.explanation: Conventional current is defined as the direction positive charge would move, which is opposite to the electrons' drift: to the right.
choiceExplanations: Moving electrons make a current even though the wire stays neutral overall.
Conventional current points opposite to the motion of negative charges.
Resistance affects the size of the current, not its direction.
